BST260 Final Project Proposal: Homicide and Firearm Mortality in the United States

Jialin Du

2026-11-17

Source: vignettes/proposal.qmd

To: BST260 Teaching Team, Fall 2026

Project overview

For my final project, I plan to examine how homicide and firearm mortality rates vary across U.S. states and over time. I am interested in whether states differ only in their mortality rates or also in how those rates change from year to year. The two measures are related but not identical, so studying them side by side may help put their geographic and temporal patterns into context. The project will focus on describing these patterns and their limitations rather than drawing causal conclusions.

Data and research questions

I will use two datasets provided with the BST260 project template: cdcmurd, which contains homicide mortality data, and cdcfiremort, which contains firearm mortality data. Both are described in the package documentation as state-level data from the CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS). The relevant CDC Stats of the States pages are Homicide Mortality and Firearm Mortality. These pages identify CDC WONDER and National Vital Statistics System mortality data as their underlying sources. I will use the versions bundled in finalproject and document their actual year ranges, variable definitions, and coverage, rather than assume that the packaged data contain all years shown on the current CDC pages.

I plan to address two questions:

  1. How is calendar year associated with the age-adjusted homicide mortality rate across U.S. states, and how do these trends differ by state?
  2. How is calendar year associated with the age-adjusted firearm mortality rate across U.S. states, and how do these trends differ by state?

The population of interest is residents of the U.S. states and District of Columbia represented in the data. The planned unit of analysis is a state-year, subject to confirming that each dataset has one record per state and year. In each analysis, the main exposure is calendar year, which I will treat as a numeric variable to summarize changes over time and as a categorical variable for comparisons between individual years. The outcome is a continuous age-adjusted mortality rate expressed as deaths per 100,000 population. State will be treated as a categorical grouping variable. In cdcmurd, the course materials identify YEAR, Location, and Death.Rate as the relevant columns; I will inspect cdcfiremort before deciding whether any variable names need to be harmonized.

Planned analysis

I will begin by inspecting the structure of each dataset and checking which states and years are represented, whether there are duplicate state-year records, and where important values are missing. I will report the number of available observations and the number of missing mortality rates by state and year. Records without a usable year or state identifier cannot be included in state-year comparisons. For summaries of mortality rates, I will exclude observations with missing rates and report those exclusions rather than treating missing values as zero. Because the CDC cautions that rates based on small numbers of deaths can be unstable or unavailable, I will check the documentation and any available death counts before interpreting missing or extreme rates.

For each dataset, I plan to summarize the distribution of state mortality rates by year using medians, quartiles, and ranges. Boxplots or dot plots will show how states compare in the same year, while line plots will show trends for individual states over time. I will also look at whether differences between states have narrowed or widened over the available years. These summaries will describe the distribution across states; for example, an unweighted average of state rates should not be interpreted as the U.S. national mortality rate.

If there are enough repeated observations across states and years, I also plan to fit an exploratory linear regression of the mortality rate on calendar year, with state indicators to account for relatively stable differences between states. I will check whether a straight-line trend is a reasonable summary and rely on year-specific plots when the pattern is not approximately linear. If I report model-based uncertainty, I will account for repeated observations from the same state. I chose state as an adjustment factor because differences in baseline conditions across states could otherwise obscure temporal comparisons. Other potentially important factors include socioeconomic conditions, firearm legislation, and changes in population composition. The packaged datasets do not necessarily measure these factors, so I will not claim that the model adjusts for them. Age adjustment helps with differences in age structure, but neither age adjustment nor state indicators remove all sources of confounding.

After analyzing the two outcomes separately, I will compare their patterns only for states and years available in both datasets. Homicide mortality includes deaths involving methods other than firearms, while firearm mortality includes suicides and other firearm-related deaths in addition to firearm homicides. Since the categories overlap, I will not add the rates or interpret their difference as a count of any particular type of death. Instead, I will describe where their overall patterns appear similar or different and consider possible explanations without treating those comparisons as causal evidence.

Planned final deliverables

I will prepare two Quarto vignettes in the finalproject R package: one analyzing cdcmurd and the other analyzing cdcfiremort. Each vignette will include the data source and provenance, any cleaning decisions, descriptive statistics and visualizations, an interpretation of the findings, and a discussion of uncertainty and limitations. I also plan to write small reusable R functions for checks and summaries that apply to both datasets. The code and vignettes will be available in the public GitHub repository, and the completed reports will be published through the package’s pkgdown website.
